opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's useful to see these as two points on a spectrum rather than separate problems. The work we've done on benchmarks like CORE-Bench was about the checking side: you take a paper, its code, and its data, and ask whether an agent can actually run the thing and reproduce the reported results. What we learned is that this is surprisingly hard, not because the science is deep, but because the computational plumbing is messy. Dependencies aren't pinned, file paths are hard-coded to someone's laptop, a script assumes you've run another script first, and none of that is written down.

That's actually what makes me optimistic about the "helping researchers make it reproducible" direction. The failure modes an agent hits when it tries to reproduce a paper are exactly the friction points a human reviewer or a future reader would hit. So if you flip it around and run that same process before publication, while the researcher still has all the context in their head, the agent becomes a kind of friendly adversary. It says: "I tried to run your pipeline in a clean environment, it broke here, here's what I think is missing." The researcher can fix that in five minutes, whereas a reader two years later might spend days on it or just give up.

I'd envision a few stages. The first is diagnostic: the agent tries to reproduce and produces a report of what went wrong. The second is assistive: it proposes concrete fixes, like generating a requirements file, a container spec, a README that documents the order of operations, and the researcher reviews and accepts them. And the more ambitious stage is integrating this into the workflow continuously, so reproducibility isn't a cleanup task at the end of a project but something that's maintained as you go, the way continuous integration works in software engineering.

But I want to add a couple of cautions. One is that an agent saying "this reproduces" is not the same as the science being correct. You can perfectly reproduce a result that's built on a flawed analysis, data leakage, a bad evaluation. Computational reproducibility is a necessary floor, not a guarantee of validity, and I'd worry about these tools creating a false sense of rigor if people treat a green checkmark as a stamp of approval.

The other is about incentives. The technical barrier was never the only barrier. Researchers often don't make their code reproducible because nobody rewards it and it takes time away from the next paper. If AI tools drive the cost down close to zero, that removes one big excuse, and that's genuinely valuable. But journals, conferences, and funders still have to decide they care. Ideally you'd see venues saying, "Run this tool, attach the report," and then the norm shifts. So I see the technology as an enabler, but whether it actually changes scientific practice depends on whether the community builds the institutions around it.

r001.rationale: The response says the same reproduction process can identify problems before publication and help researchers fix them quickly, including proposing concrete fixes. This clearly conveys that helping with reproducibility should not be much harder once checking is possible.

r002.rationale: The response mentions generating a requirements file and container spec and integrating reproducibility checks into the workflow, but it does not propose integrating LLMs into software packaging systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think of this as a progression with a few distinct stages, and we're really only at the first one right now.

The first stage is verification. You take a paper, you take the code repository that goes with it, and you ask: can an agent actually run this and get the numbers in the paper? That turns out to be surprisingly hard even for humans, because the README is incomplete, the environment is underspecified, there's some data file that was never uploaded, and so on. And what we've found is that agents are actually pretty good at the grunt work of this. They'll try to install dependencies, they'll notice that a package version doesn't match, they'll go hunting for the missing file. So the near-term value is just scaling up reproducibility checks, which today almost nobody does because it's so tedious. Journals don't do it, reviewers don't do it, and so we have this situation where a lot of published computational research is not reproducible and nobody knows which parts.

The second stage, and this is where I think it gets more interesting, is diagnosis. It's not enough to say "this didn't reproduce." The agent should be able to say why. Was it a seed that wasn't set? Was it data leakage between train and test, which is a huge problem in machine-learning-based science specifically? Was it a preprocessing step that the authors did by hand and never documented? Those are very different failures with very different fixes, and distinguishing them requires actually reading the code with some understanding of what the research is trying to do, not just running it.

And then the third stage is the one you're asking about, which is helping the researcher upstream. Right now reproducibility is something that gets checked, if at all, after the fact. What I'd like to see is the assistant sitting with you while you write the analysis and saying, look, you're loading this file from a hardcoded path on your laptop, that's not going to work for anyone else. Or, you computed this feature using the whole dataset before splitting, that's leakage. Or just, here's a Dockerfile that captures your environment, here's a script that regenerates every figure in the paper from scratch. A lot of that is boring, and researchers don't do it because it's boring and there's no incentive, and that's exactly the kind of thing LLMs are good for.

I do want to add two cautions though. One is that the reason reproducibility is bad is mostly not a tooling problem, it's an incentive problem. Nobody gets tenure for a clean repository. So the technology can lower the cost, but it doesn't change the fact that there's very little reward. The second is that if agents become the thing that certifies reproducibility, people will optimize for passing the agent, and that's not the same as the science being right. Reproducible and correct are different properties. You can have code that runs perfectly and produces exactly the numbers in the paper, and the analysis is still flawed. So I think of this as helping with one necessary condition, not as a substitute for the human judgment about whether the research actually supports the claims.

r001.rationale: The response describes LLMs helping researchers improve reproducibility, but does not say that fixing problems should be no harder than checking for them.

r002.rationale: It mentions generating a Dockerfile and a script, but does not propose integrating LLMs into software packaging systems.

astra-6.text:
I think the important shift is from identifying a problem to helping close the loop. Checking reproducibility might tell you, “This dependency is missing,” or, “I ran the code, but I didn’t get the number reported in the paper.” That’s useful, but the researcher still has to figure out why and what to change.

An LLM assistant could help with those next steps: identifying assumptions about the environment, suggesting fixes, making the setup instructions explicit, and then rerunning the experiment to see whether those changes actually work. Ideally, that assistance happens while you’re doing the research, rather than becoming a big cleanup task when you’re ready to release the code.

The key distinction is between making the code run and making the research reproducible. An assistant could get a program to execute by changing something that matters scientifically. So we need a process where changes are visible, researchers retain control over those decisions, and the evidence comes from executing and checking the experiments—not just from the model saying that it fixed the problem.

r001.rationale: The response says an LLM could help identify assumptions, suggest fixes, and rerun experiments, but it does not state that fixing reproducibility problems should be about as easy as checking them.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose integrating LLMs into software packaging systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the next step is to move from diagnosis to an interactive process. Instead of simply saying, “I couldn’t reproduce this result,” the assistant could help identify what’s missing. Is there a dependency that wasn’t specified? Is there a preprocessing step that’s described in the paper but absent from the code? Are there assumptions about the computing environment that the authors haven’t documented?

Then it could work with the researcher to address those issues: construct the environment, clarify the instructions, add a small test, and actually rerun the analysis to see whether the changes worked. That last part is essential. Generating a plausible fix isn’t the same as demonstrating that the result is reproducible.

And ideally, this happens while the research is being done, rather than at the end when someone is trying to reconstruct what happened six months earlier. I think there’s a real opportunity to make reproducibility a byproduct of the research workflow. But we also have to distinguish reproducing a number from establishing that the underlying scientific claim is valid. An assistant can help with both, potentially, but those are different tasks.

r001.rationale: The response describes moving from diagnosis to interactive help fixing reproducibility issues, but does not say that fixing them should be not much harder than checking.

r002.rationale: It mentions constructing an environment and clarifying instructions, but does not propose integrating LLMs into software packaging systems.
